stem: (Select TWO.) Solvent Analytics' five engineers currently trust whoever last touched the servers to remember what is actually running, and nobody double-checks an edit before it goes live. Leadership wants a second set of eyes on every edit, and a way for any of the five to check what is actually running without asking that person. Which two actions meet both needs?

choices.text: Put the configuration in a version-controlled repository and require a pull-request approval before any edit is merged.
Push settings to the servers directly from whichever engineer's laptop is making the change, using a configuration-management tool with no shared review step in between.
Keep the configuration file only on the laptop of whoever wrote it most recently, and announce changes in a chat channel.
Keep the record of what already exists in a location every engineer's tooling can read, not only on the machine of whoever last ran a change.
Apply the configuration from whichever engineer's laptop is making the change, with the resulting record of what was built kept only on that engineer's own machine.

rationale: A version-controlled repository with required pull-request approval is the second-set-of-eyes half of the requirement. Keeping the built-infrastructure record somewhere every engineer's own tooling can read, rather than on one person's machine, is the shared-visibility half, which is what HCP Terraform's shared state adds on top of plain version control. Pushing settings straight from a laptop through a configuration-management tool has no review gate at all. Keeping the file on only one person's laptop and announcing changes in chat is exactly the problem the stem describes. Applying from a laptop with the record of what was built kept on that same machine leaves every other engineer unable to see what is actually running without asking.
